claims.text: In high-entropy superconducting alloys, Tc is primarily governed by electron scattering at grain boundaries.
Nanocrystallinity and lattice distortions in a random solid solution induce the grain-boundary scattering that governs Tc.
The proposed initial state is an as-deposited nanocrystalline high-entropy alloy with a grain size of approximately 20 nm.
The as-deposited alloy is a disordered or random solid solution.
The approximately 20 nm microstructure has a significant grain-boundary density.
Controlled annealing will coarsen the grains.
Grain coarsening by annealing will reduce grain-boundary density.
The as-deposited and annealed states can be compared while holding alloy composition and deposition conditions constant.
Random-solid-solution structure produces lattice distortions associated with grain boundaries.
A high grain-boundary density enhances electron scattering.
Enhanced electron scattering disrupts Cooper-pair formation and depresses Tc.
Annealed samples with larger grains will have lower electron-scattering rates than as-deposited nanocrystalline samples.
Annealed samples with larger grains will have a higher Tc than as-deposited nanocrystalline samples.
The proposed effect should be significant in high-entropy alloys whose superconductivity is influenced by disorder and nanostructuring.
The proposed relationship may not extend to bulk single crystals or alloys with inherently low lattice distortion.
Failure of annealing to produce both a statistically significant Tc increase and a corresponding scattering-rate decrease would falsify the proposed mechanism.
